name: Presbyterian Church (USA)
summary: A Presbyterian church formed in 1983 by reunion of the northern UPCUSA and southern PCUS traditions.

key_figures.role: moderator associated with the northern church at reunion
key_figures.summary: moderator associated with the northern church at reunion. This role should be read in the formation and development described above, rather than as a claim of sole authorship of the tradition.

key_dates.label: Belhar Confession added to the Book of Confessions

formation_narrative: The 1983 reunion sought to reunite major American Presbyterian streams divided since the Civil War era and to strengthen shared ministry. It joined institutions with overlapping Reformed ancestry but distinct histories. The resulting church uses a collection of confessional witnesses rather than reducing its identity to one theologian. Its continuing internal diversity requires care when explaining social policy or theological orientation; a blanket Barthian label is inadequate.
core_beliefs: God’s grace and sovereignty: salvation is understood as God’s initiative in Christ rather than a human achievement.
Scripture and confession: the Bible is the primary norm; confessions and catechisms explain the church’s accountable reading of it.
Church and sacraments: preaching, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper belong to a disciplined Christian community, with government through ministers and elders in Presbyterian forms.

key_documents.title: Book of Confessions
key_documents.significance: Constitutional collection of creeds, confessions, and catechisms from different periods; it is not a claim that every statement originated in 1983.

key_documents.title: Confession of Belhar
key_documents.significance: South African confession addressing unity, reconciliation, and justice; received by PCUSA in 2016.

name: Presbyterian Church in America
summary: A conservative Reformed Presbyterian denomination organized in 1973 by churches leaving the PCUS.

key_figures.name: Morton H. Smith
key_figures.role: Reformed theologian and founding stated clerk of the PCA, serving 1973–1988; distinct from Morton Smith the ancient historian
key_figures.summary: Morton Howison Smith was a Reformed theologian and the PCA’s first stated clerk (1973–1988), responsible for important early administrative continuity. He is a different person from Morton Smith, the Columbia ancient historian associated with the Secret Gospel of Mark debate.

key_figures.name: W. Jack Williamson
key_figures.summary: A Presbyterian leader associated with the PCA’s founding generation. His inclusion concerns organizational beginnings rather than authorship of the whole Reformed tradition.

key_dates.label: PCA organized and first General Assembly meets

formation_narrative: Organizers opposed what they regarded as theological liberalism and weakening commitment to biblical and Reformed teaching in the PCUS. They sought a church explicitly committed to Scripture, Westminster doctrine, and evangelistic mission. Those are the founders’ stated aims, not a neutral verdict on the Christianity of everyone who remained. The new church organized representative courts and a General Assembly; Morton H. Smith helped establish its continuing administration.
core_beliefs: Reformed doctrine: the Westminster Confession and catechisms summarize its reading of biblical teaching.
Biblical authority and mission: the denomination identifies fidelity to Scripture and evangelistic work as core purposes.
Presbyterian government: local sessions, regional presbyteries, and the General Assembly share responsibility through representative elders.

key_documents.significance: Historic Reformed doctrinal and teaching texts. American revisions and each church’s subscription rules must be distinguished from the original Scottish form.

name: Orthodox Presbyterian Church
summary: A confessional Presbyterian church founded in 1936 during disputes over theology, mission, and authority in the PCUSA.

key_figures.name: J. Gresham Machen
key_figures.role: New Testament scholar, Westminster Seminary founder, and leading organizer of the church
key_figures.summary: A New Testament scholar formerly at Princeton, founder of Westminster Theological Seminary, and leading figure in the 1936 Presbyterian separation.

key_dates.label: Name changed to Orthodox Presbyterian Church

formation_narrative: Machen and colleagues believed modernist teaching had undermined the church’s doctrinal and missionary witness. Their conflict with the PCUSA produced a separate body in June 1936, first called the Presbyterian Church of America. The name changed in 1939 under legal pressure. The OPC’s own historical account presents its separation as preservation of historic Christianity; that evaluation should be attributed rather than assigned to all historians or all parties.
core_beliefs: Westminster subscription: the confession and catechisms are subordinate standards under Scripture.
Reformed salvation: teaching emphasizes God’s sovereignty and Christ’s saving work rather than human merit.
Ordered church life: ministers and elders govern through sessions, presbyteries, and assemblies; doctrinal discipline and missions remain closely connected.

key_documents.title: Westminster Confession and Catechisms
key_documents.significance: The OPC receives an American revised form; its account explicitly distinguishes revisions it accepts from PCUSA changes it did not adopt.

name: Presbyterian Church in the United States
summary: The southern Presbyterian denomination formed in the Civil War era and reunited with UPCUSA in 1983.

key_figures.role: moderator of the first southern General Assembly in 1861
key_figures.summary: A southern Presbyterian preacher selected as moderator of the first Confederate-era General Assembly. His role belongs in the context of church organization, secession, and slavery rather than being reduced to an honorary founder label.

key_figures.summary: reunion-era moderator associated with PCUS. This role should be read in the formation and development described above, rather than as a claim of sole authorship of the tradition.

key_dates.label: PCA organizes from departing PCUS churches

formation_narrative: The national crisis over slavery and federal union divided Presbyterians as well as the country. Southern Presbyterians organized the Presbyterian Church in the Confederate States of America in 1861; the body later used the PCUS name. Shared Reformed doctrine did not erase political and moral differences. A conservative departure created the PCA in 1973, but the PCUS itself continued until its 1983 reunion with the northern UPCUSA.

Scripture and confession: the Bible is the primary norm; confessions and catechisms explain the church’s accountable reading of it.

name: Presbyterian Church in the United States of America
notes: Merged into UPCUSA in 1958. The national body began before the Civil War; “Northern” describes its later sectional history, not all of its membership in 1789.
summary: The national Presbyterian body whose first General Assembly met in 1789 and whose later northern history led to UPCUSA.

key_figures.name: Francis Makemie
key_figures.role: earlier presbyterial organizer in the church’s ancestry
key_figures.summary: An Irish-born Presbyterian minister who served colonial communities and helped organize early American presbyterial cooperation.

key_figures.name: Eugene Carson Blake
key_figures.role: stated clerk and advocate of the 1958 union
key_figures.summary: A Presbyterian stated clerk and advocate of ecumenical cooperation who helped advance the 1958 union creating UPCUSA.

key_dates.label: Constitutional organization and American confessional revisions

formation_narrative: Colonial presbyteries and synods developed national structures after American independence. Constitutional organization in 1788 and the first General Assembly in 1789 are distinct milestones. Subsequent disputes over revival, theology, slavery, and mission produced separations and reunions. Calling the entire 1789 body simply northern projects a later sectional identity backward. It joined the UPCNA in 1958 rather than becoming the present PCUSA directly.
core_beliefs: God’s grace and sovereignty: salvation is understood as God’s initiative in Christ rather than a human achievement.
Scripture and confession: the Bible is the primary norm; confessions and catechisms explain the church’s accountable reading of it.
Church and sacraments: preaching, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper belong to a disciplined Christian community, with government through ministers and elders in Presbyterian forms.

key_documents.significance: Adapted the inherited confession for the American setting; later PCUSA revisions and OPC reception differ.

key_dates.label: PCUSA and UPCNA unite on May 28
Confession of 1967 expands the church’s confessional framework
Reunites with PCUS to form PCUSA

formation_narrative: Union advocates sought stronger shared ministry across previously distinct Reformed institutions. Eugene Carson Blake promoted ecumenical cooperation, while some UPCNA members worried about losing their independent identity. The new denomination assembled in Pittsburgh in May 1958. It subsequently broadened its confessional collection and in 1983 joined the PCUS to form the present PCUSA. The merger did not mean every congregation agreed equally with every motive.

name: United Presbyterian Church of North America
notes: Merger partner in 1958 formation of UPCUSA.
summary: A Presbyterian denomination formed in 1858 from Associate and Reformed Presbyterian streams and merged into UPCUSA in 1958.

key_figures.name: Samuel W. Shane
key_figures.summary: The UPCNA stated clerk at the 1958 union, later serving as associate stated clerk in the new denomination.

key_figures.role: moderator of the final UPCNA assembly
key_figures.summary: moderator of the final UPCNA assembly. This role should be read in the formation and development described above, rather than as a claim of sole authorship of the tradition.

key_figures.role: former UPCNA missionary and first moderator of the successor UPCUSA
key_figures.summary: A former UPCNA missionary and seminary professor elected first moderator of UPCUSA, symbolizing the participation of both uniting churches.

key_dates.label: Constituted by union of two older churches

formation_narrative: The Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church and Associate Presbyterian Church of North America united in 1858, seeking common Presbyterian ministry across previously separate institutions. The northern Associate Reformed stream must be distinguished from continuing southern ARP church life. A century later union with the larger PCUSA promised broader ministry but prompted concern about independence and continuity. The 1958 merger ended UPCNA as a separate body and created UPCUSA; both its own formation and its eventual union matter to the lineage.
core_beliefs: Reformed inheritance: Westminster teaching supplied a common doctrinal language for the uniting traditions.
Presbyterian order: congregations participated through elders, presbyteries, and wider assemblies.

Distinctive identity and union: members disagreed about how confessional continuity should relate to wider Presbyterian cooperation; the earlier exclusive-psalmody label needs its own detailed historical sourcing.

key_documents.significance: Historic Reformed doctrinal and teaching texts. American revisions and each church’s subscription rules must be distinguished from the original Scottish form.

profile_scope: The Westminster link explains inherited doctrine; original 1858 union standards and changes to worship practice remain research priorities.
ending_narrative: UPCNA entered the 1958 union with PCUSA to form UPCUSA. Supporters sought a wider common ministry, while substantial internal opposition reflected concern about independence and identity. The main body ceased as a separate denomination; the source records limited provision for opting out rather than universal unanimity.
